claim: COVID-19 took away critical training opportunities from those looking to enter the industries.

quotes: I can add to that the education bodies that trained artists and technicians and designers online over COVID. They are coming into our theatre because we are a training ground for those people, and their physical skill knowledge is so below what it would have been had they been able to do practical work. That then leaves them with anxiety because they do not know or, you know, then they are leaving the industry. So they have done all that study and they are leaving. There are a lot of challenges post COVID from that disconnection from reality.
The lack of technical people that can do technical work – they have left the industry because they were not supported.
detail.critic_finding: Sources support that COVID degraded practical training quality for arts/theatre students and technicians, but the claim's broad framing ("those looking to enter the industries") overstates the scope beyond what the passages specifically address.
detail.source_says: COVID forced arts training online, leaving emerging theatre artists and technicians with below-standard practical skills, causing anxiety and attrition from the sector.
detail.so_what: Reader would miss that the claim is specifically about theatre/arts trainees whose practical skills were degraded by online-only training, not a broad cross-industry training loss.

claim: COVID-19 led to worsening mental health in the industries, particularly among children and young people.

quotes: what we have seen in pulling together that work and other works is the incredible rise in young people who are suffering various forms of social anxiety. You know, school refusal – I think that is the term where they are just not going or they are not fitting a pattern that was previously seen as a normal way for young people to be responding. And I think there is reasonable evidence that much of that can be seen as a result of the isolation caused through COVID.
The mental health impact afterwards on artists was quite profound.

Financial precarity was already an issue for artists generally before the COVID lockdowns, but the intensity and duration of lockdowns in Melbourne significantly depressed the creative economy, and the ensuing cost of living as well as housing affordability has resulted in high rates of depression and mental health and wellbeing issues among these groups.
detail.critic_finding: Multiple witnesses directly attribute worsened mental health—anxiety, depression, social anxiety—to COVID-19, with particular emphasis on young people. The summary accurately and proportionately reflects the testimony.

claim: Witnesses said ticket prices have fallen since 2019.

quotes: A cost-of-living crisis means that while audiences are returning, ticket prices remain stagnant, limiting income.
2.1 million fewer people have attended fewer events in the last five years, with 47 per cent citing the ticket prices and 38 per cent citing the cost of living as a cause.

the only way we can meet these increasing costs is obviously by increasing our ticket prices. That then, conversely, reduces our audience numbers due to the lack of affordability for them to attend our shows
detail.critic_finding: Witnesses describe ticket prices as stagnant (Lowe) or increasing (Cunningham), not falling. No passage supports a fall in ticket prices since 2019.
detail.so_what: Readers would believe ticket prices dropped, when witnesses said they are stagnant or rising, limiting income.

claim: Victoria receives its fair share of funding from Creative Australia.

quotes: Victoria is the only state or territory that is getting exactly its fair share on a per capita basis. You have 26 per cent of the population, and our analysis shows that you are getting 26 per cent of Creative Australia money.

when we cut the data from Creative Australia by region using the accessibility/remoteness index of Australia – ARIA – definition, which has 40 per cent of Australians living in regional Australia, the total of Creative Australia's investment that goes to regional is 17 per cent, so 23 per cent less than what they should be getting.
detail.critic_finding: Kate Fielding confirms Victoria as a whole gets its per-capita share from Creative Australia, but the same witness and others make clear regional Victoria gets far less than its share — a critical distinction the summary omits.
detail.source_says: Victoria as a whole receives exactly its per-capita share (26%) of Creative Australia funding, but regional Victoria receives only 17% of Creative Australia investment against a 40% population share — described as "severely inadequate."
detail.so_what: Reader would miss that "fair share" applies only to Victoria overall, not to regional Victoria, which is severely underfunded.

claim: Regional Victoria does not receive its fair share of funding from Creative Australia.

quotes: Victoria is the only state or territory that is getting exactly its fair share on a per capita basis. You have 26 per cent of the population, and our analysis shows that you are getting 26 per cent of Creative Australia money.

when we cut the data from Creative Australia by region using the accessibility/remoteness index of Australia – ARIA – definition, which has 40 per cent of Australians living in regional Australia, the total of Creative Australia's investment that goes to regional is 17 per cent, so 23 per cent less than what they should be getting.
detail.critic_finding: Kate Fielding explicitly states Victoria as a whole gets exactly its per-capita share from Creative Australia. The underfunding finding applies specifically to regional areas nationally (17% vs 40% population share), not to Victoria overall.
detail.source_says: Victoria as a whole receives exactly its per-capita share (26%) from Creative Australia. However, regionally, only 17% of Creative Australia investment goes to regional Australia despite 40% of Australians living there; and within Victoria, regional areas are considered considerably underinvested relative to Melbourne.
detail.so_what: Victoria overall gets its exact per-capita share from Creative Australia; the shortfall is specific to regional areas within Victoria, not Victoria as a whole.

claim: Regional Victoria receives its fair share of funding from Creative Australia.

quotes: From our analysis of that – and this is just Creative Australia – Victoria is the only state or territory that is getting exactly its fair share on a per capita basis. You have 26 per cent of the population, and our analysis shows that you are getting 26 per cent of Creative Australia money.

when we cut the data from Creative Australia by region using the accessibility/remoteness index of Australia – ARIA – definition, which has 40 per cent of Australians living in regional Australia, the total of Creative Australia's investment that goes to regional is 17 per cent, so 23 per cent less than what they should be getting.
Certainly not, Gaelle, and thank you very much for the question.
detail.critic_finding: The "fair share" finding applies to Victoria as a whole (state-level), not regional Victoria. Multiple witnesses explicitly state regional Victoria is severely underfunded, with only 17% of Creative Australia investment vs. 40% population share.
detail.source_says: Victoria as a whole receives exactly its per-capita share (26%) of Creative Australia funding, but regional Victoria specifically receives only 17% of Creative Australia investment—23 percentage points below its population share—and witnesses describe regional Victoria's share as "absolutely inadequate."
detail.so_what: Readers would think regional Victoria gets its fair share; in fact witnesses say it is significantly underfunded relative to population.

claim: According to Claire Febey of Creative Victoria, COVID-19 led to worsening mental health in the industries, particularly among children and young people.

detail.critic_finding: Claire Febey's passages contain no statement about COVID-19 causing worsening mental health, especially among children or young people. Those observations came from other witnesses (Mullings, Cunningham, Champion, Toulson, Dullard).
detail.so_what: Reader would think Claire Febey testified about COVID's mental health impact on youth, but she never did.
